title: Remount
teaches: The remount as we trade it: a leader loses a line for real, an average or a price level it held, then retakes it with a clear green close. We buy after a quiet day holds above the line, with a market order over that day's high and a real stop a few cents under its low. The close must be above the 200-day, a third comes off at 3R and 5R, and most tries lose small.

questions.q: In one line, what is a Remount?
choices: Retaking a line it really lost
A one-day dip under yesterday's low
A flat-base breakout on heavy volume
A bounce off a rising 50-day average
questions.answer: Retaking a line it really lost
questions.why: Retaking a line it really lost. The stock lost it for real, then took it back. A short dip never really lost the line, so that is a pullback or a U&R, not a Remount.
questions.lesson_line: A Remount is a line lost for real, then taken back.

wrong.A one-day dip under yesterday's low: That is closer to an Oops, one session. A Remount follows a line lost for real.
wrong.A flat-base breakout on heavy volume: No line was lost first. A Remount buys back a line the stock really lost.
wrong.A bounce off a rising 50-day average: A bounce never really lost the line. A Remount buys back a line the stock really lost.

reasons: +2 what 'lost for real' means rests on a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: The Remount has two kinds of line: the 50-day or 200-day, and a price level that held.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The Remount has two forms. The average form is a lost and retaken 50-day or 200-day. The level form is a pivot, base low, old high or round number that held before it broke. It is one setup with two kinds of line.
questions.lesson_line: One setup, two kinds of line: an average or a level.
questions.simple: True. The Remount can use the 50-day or 200-day, or a price level that held before it broke.

questions.q: Which averages does the moving-average form use?
choices: The 50-day and the 200-day lines
The 5-day and the 8-day lines
The 100-day and the 150-day lines
The 10-day and the 21-day lines
questions.answer: The 50-day and the 200-day lines
questions.why: The 50-day and the 200-day lines. If the stock lost and retook one of them, it is the moving-average form. The 10-day and the 21-day are our trail lines for selling.
questions.lesson_line: The moving-average form: the 50-day or the 200-day.

wrong.The 5-day and the 8-day lines: Those short lines are not the moving-average form's lines. It is the 50-day and the 200-day.
wrong.The 100-day and the 150-day lines: Neither is a line of the moving-average form. It is the 50-day and the 200-day.
wrong.The 10-day and the 21-day lines: Those are our trail lines for selling the last third. The moving-average form is the 50-day and the 200-day.

questions.simple: The moving-average form uses the 50-day and the 200-day lines, not the short trail lines.

reasons: +2 which lines count rests on a held decision (D-073)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: You may buy a Remount before the close is above the line to get a better price.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Wait for the close above the line. Buying before the close is above the line, or on a marginal poke a few cents over it, is a listed mistake. ChartSchool says the same about any average cross: wait for a full candle close above it.
questions.lesson_line: No close above the line, no Remount. Do not anticipate.
questions.simple: False. The retake only counts once the day closes above the line, so buying early means buying a retake that has not happened.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We never buy a Remount with the close below the ___-day SMA.
questions.why: 200. We never buy a Remount with the close below the 200-day SMA. A 200-day remount is the cross itself.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, every time.
questions.simple: The close must be above the 200-day average, and we do not buy a Remount below it.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook (no longs below the 200-day)

questions.q: A Remount buy is a limit order, and the stop is a real order with the broker.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Entries are market orders, not limit orders. The stop is a real order with the broker, so only the first half of the statement is wrong. A stop kept in your head is not a stop. We buy in regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Market order in, real stop order out.
questions.simple: False. We buy with a market order, not a limit order, although the real stop with the broker is right.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, D41)

questions.q: A successful Remount turns the line from a ceiling back into a floor.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. After a stock loses a line, the line can act as a ceiling. IBD notes stocks often need a large boost of buying power to muscle back above a lost 50-day line. A clean retake turns the ceiling back into a floor. That is the idea, not a promise: the line can be lost again, and the stop takes the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A lost line can be a ceiling. A clean retake makes it a floor.
questions.simple: True. A line a stock lost can act like a ceiling, and a clean retake makes it a floor again.

questions.q: A 50-day reclaim counts only if the close is also above the 200-day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A 50-day reclaim counts only with the close above the 200-day too. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. ChartSchool makes the same point: look for bullish crosses only when price is already above the longer average.
questions.lesson_line: A fifty-day retake needs the 200-day under you first.
questions.simple: True. We do not buy below the 200-day, so a 50-day retake counts only when the close is also above the 200-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, a hard rule)

questions.q: What does IBD say institutions may do once a stock is below its 50-day?
choices: Use the line to mark a sell level
Treat the line as a floor to buy
Wait for the 200-day before acting
Add to longs as price nears the line
questions.answer: Use the line to mark a sell level
questions.why: Use the line to mark a sell level. IBD says that once a stock is below its 50-day line, institutional investors may use it to mark a sell level. It also says stocks often need a large boost of buying power to muscle back above it. IBD says may, not will.
questions.lesson_line: A lost line can become a sell level. Retaking it takes real buying.

wrong.Treat the line as a floor to buy: IBD says the opposite: below the line, institutions may use it to mark a sell level.
wrong.Wait for the 200-day before acting: IBD's point is about the 50-day line itself, which institutions may use to mark a sell level.
wrong.Add to longs as price nears the line: IBD says institutions may use the line to mark where they sell, not where they add.

questions.simple: Institutions may use a lost 50-day line to mark where they sell, so retaking it takes real buying.

reasons: the key rests on one cited IBD quote (i2)

questions.q: A Remount counts once price pokes a few cents over the line during the day.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A remount needs a full candle close above the line. ChartSchool says to wait for a full candle close above the average before calling a cross. A marginal poke a few cents over the line during the day is not a remount day, and buying it is a listed mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Close it above. A poke is not a retake.
questions.simple: False. A retake counts only when the day closes above the line, not when price touches it for a moment.

questions.q: IBD reads a weak, low-volume rise after a high-volume drop under the 50-day as what?
choices: A chance to sell
A Remount to buy
A reason to add
A confirmed bottom
questions.answer: A chance to sell
questions.why: A chance to sell. IBD says a high-volume decline to or below the 50-day, followed by a weak low-volume rise, is your chance to sell. A stock often needs a large boost of buying power to muscle back above a lost 50-day line. A light rise does not show it. So it is not a Remount to buy, and our card lists buying that drift as a mistake.
questions.lesson_line: A light drift back after a heavy drop is a sell, not a buy.

wrong.A Remount to buy: IBD says the opposite. A light rise after a heavy drop is a sell, and our card lists it as a mistake.
wrong.A reason to add: A weak rise gives no reason to add.
wrong.A confirmed bottom: A weak, low-volume rise confirms nothing.

questions.simple: IBD reads it as a chance to sell, because a weak rise on low volume lacks the buying power to retake the line.

reasons: the light-volume invalidation is proposed on card 13 and held (D-006)

questions.q: A Remount on the earnings reaction day is allowed, because the report is already out.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A remount on the earnings gap itself is after the report, so it is allowed. The block is on new buys in the 3 sessions before a report. AMD remounted its 50-day on the reaction day, with the report out after the close on 2023-10-31. It does not mean a buy just before a report is fine.
questions.lesson_line: After the report is fine. Before it is not.
questions.simple: True. The report is already out on the reaction day, so the ban on buying before a report does not apply.

deeper.example: AMD reported after the close on 2023-10-31. On 2023-11-01, the reaction day, it closed back over its 50-day. The buy point was 109.41. The buy came on 2023-11-03 at 109.42 with the stop at 105.86, 3.3% away, and its best run was 21.2R. One example is not a promise: most tries lose small.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, no buys in the 3 days before a report)

questions.q: What most separates a Remount from a U&R (Undercut and Rally)?
choices: How long the line stayed lost
How heavy the volume was
Whether the 200-day was rising
Whether it gapped on earnings
questions.answer: How long the line stayed lost
questions.why: How long the line stayed lost. A U&R is back above the line within a few sessions. A Remount lost its line for real before the retake. A gap on earnings or a rising 200-day does not name the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions under the line. A quick return is a U&R, a real stay a Remount.

wrong.How heavy the volume was: Volume helps judge the retake, but it does not name the setup. The time under the line does.
wrong.Whether the 200-day was rising: A rising 200-day is a grade cue, not what splits a Remount from a U&R.
wrong.Whether it gapped on earnings: A remount on the earnings gap is allowed and is still a Remount. The gap does not split the two.

questions.simple: The split is how long the line stayed lost, since a U&R is back above within a few sessions.

reasons: +2 the border between the two setups is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Move the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first ___ by default.
questions.answer: trim
questions.why: Trim. The stop goes to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: First trim, stop to breakeven.

questions.q: Buy 86.24, stop 83.52. How far is the stop below the buy, in percent?
questions.why: 3.2%. Take the buy minus the stop. Divide that by the buy, 86.24, to get about 3.2%. That is PYPL, just over the 3% a stop usually sits within, so the size comes down.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you size the trade.
questions.simple: The gap from buy to stop, divided by the buy, is about 3.2 percent, just over the usual 3 percent.

reasons: +2 computed key

questions.q: Bought at 109.42 with the stop at 105.86. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 120.10. One R is the fill minus the stop. Three R is three of those. Add them to the fill, 109.42, to get 120.10. The first third comes off there.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open.
questions.simple: Three R is three times the gap between the 109.42 fill and the stop, added to the fill.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the third at 3R is a rulebook rule

questions.q: A close back under the line after the buy is an extra exit before the stop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit. A close back under the line is not an extra exit; the trade is held while it stays above the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit. A close under the line is a warning only.

questions.q: What kind of stop do we place on a Remount?
choices: A broker order under the low
A close-only stop under the low
A mental stop under the low
No stop until it is up 1R
questions.answer: A broker order under the low
questions.why: A broker order under the low. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, set a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. The stop comes first, then the size. It only moves up. A stop kept in your head does not count.
questions.lesson_line: A real order, a few cents under the low.

wrong.A close-only stop under the low: A stop that waits for a close is not a real order with the broker.
wrong.A mental stop under the low: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
wrong.No stop until it is up 1R: The stop comes first, before the size. It is never optional.

questions.simple: We use a real stop order with the broker, set a few cents under the low, never one kept in your head.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, F62)
which low anchors the stop is held (D-008)

questions.q: A gap through the stop is the Remount's main failure.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Chop around the line is the Remount's main failure, not a gap through the stop. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days and frees the money. ChartSchool says crossover signals are more uncertain and less reliable in sideways markets. A gap can still happen, but the card does not call it the main failure.
questions.lesson_line: Chop kills Remounts. The time stop frees the money.
questions.simple: False. The main failure is chop, where price drifts sideways around the line with no clear trend.

questions.q: After the remount day, what arms the buy?
choices: A quiet inside day above the line
Any red day with heavy volume
A second wide green day, big volume
A fresh close back under the line
questions.answer: A quiet inside day above the line
questions.why: A quiet inside day above the line. After the remount day, the pause closes above the line and ends on an inside day. The buy is a market order as price trades over that day's high. A close back under the line first means no trade.
questions.lesson_line: Retake, pause, then buy over the quiet day's high.

wrong.Any red day with heavy volume: Heavy volume is not a quiet day. The pause is an inside day that closes above the line.
wrong.A second wide green day, big volume: A wide day is not quiet. The pause is a quiet inside day that holds above the line.
wrong.A fresh close back under the line: A close back under the line before the trigger means no trade.

questions.simple: The buy is armed by a quiet inside day that holds above the line, and we buy over that day's high.

reasons: the pause entry is card 13's proposed Entry B, held (D-003)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On a normal day, the stop only moves ___.
questions.answer: up
questions.why: Up. The stop is the exit and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule. On a gap-down day, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: Up, never wider.
questions.simple: The stop only moves up, never down or wider, apart from the one gap rule.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook

questions.q: Our floors are $10 a share and $20 million a day. A $9 stock trading $30 million a day passes both.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Both tests must pass. The $30 million volume passes. The $9 price fails.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars and twenty million a day. Both.
questions.simple: A $9 stock fails the $10 price floor, even though its $30 million a day beats the $20 million volume test.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A pullback or U&R; line not lost
A Remount; the 50-day was retaken
An Oops; it was a one-session dip
A new base; the 50-day is lost
questions.answer: A pullback or U&R; line not lost
questions.why: A pullback or a U&R. The stock closed under the 50-day for only two sessions, so the line was never really lost. A Remount needs the line lost for real first. The strong candle back does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: A two-day dip is not a lost line.

wrong.A Remount; the 50-day was retaken: It retook the line, but the line was never really lost. Two closes under is a dip.
wrong.An Oops; it was a one-session dip: An Oops is one session that opens under the prior close. This took two closes under.
wrong.A new base; the 50-day is lost: A base is a long stay under the line, not a two-session dip.

questions.story: A leader closes under its 50-day for two sessions. Then it closes back above with a strong candle.
questions.simple: It is a pullback or a U&R, because two closes under the 50-day is a dip and not a lost line.

reasons: +2 what counts as a lost line is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: The AVWAP reclaim
A 50-day Remount
A flat-level Remount
An Oops, one session
questions.answer: The AVWAP reclaim
questions.why: The AVWAP reclaim. A line that starts at one event day and bends with volume is the AVWAP. A Remount's line is a moving average or a flat price level that held before it broke. The 50-day and 200-day do not start at an event day, and a flat level does not bend.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line. A bending line from an event day is not a Remount.

wrong.A 50-day Remount: A Remount uses the 50-day or the 200-day, which do not start at one event day.
wrong.A flat-level Remount: A level Remount uses a flat price level that held. This line bends with volume.
wrong.An Oops, one session: An Oops is one session that opens under the prior close. It has no line like this.

questions.story: A stock closes over a line that starts at its August high and bends with volume.
questions.simple: It is the AVWAP reclaim, because the line starts at one event day and bends with volume, which a Remount line does not.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (k20)

questions.q: Bought at 59.54, stop 58.44. If the stock trades to 61.47, how many R is that?
questions.why: 1.75R. One R is the fill minus the stop. The gain is the exit price minus the fill. Divide the gain by one R to get 1.75R. That is short of the 3R trim.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R. Under 3R, no trim.
questions.simple: R is the gain divided by the risk per share, and here that is about 1.75R, short of 3R.

deeper.example: DOCU bought at 59.54 and a gap under the stop on day 1 ended the trade. The stock then held its 50-day for 20 sessions and traded up to 61.47, which is +1.75R. It never reached 3R. The level was right and the trigger did not run.

reasons: +2 computed key

questions.q: What is the call?
choices: Fewer shares, same risk, or skip
Tighten the stop so full size fits
Buy full size and accept the extra risk
Use a stop on a close under the line
questions.answer: Fewer shares, same risk, or skip
questions.why: Size down or skip, and never tighten the stop. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. Here the honest stop is 5.5% away, so the size comes from that stop: fewer shares, the same account risk. If it still does not fit the risk, skip.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop means fewer shares or no trade. Never tighten it.

wrong.Tighten the stop so full size fits: Never tighten the stop to fit. A stop that does not mark the real low is not honest.
wrong.Buy full size and accept the extra risk: The size comes from the stop. A wide stop means fewer shares or no trade.
wrong.Use a stop on a close under the line: A stop on a close is not a real order with the broker, and it does not fix the distance.

questions.story: A clean Remount sets up. The honest stop, a few cents under the low, is 5.5% below the buy.
questions.simple: Cut the size so the risk stays the same, or skip the trade. Never tighten the stop to make a bigger size fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13)

questions.q: Gap through the stop. Your move?
choices: Get out; the loss is past 2R
Hold; 44.40 is now your stop
Wait; the 46.00 stop still rules
Buy more; the price is lower
questions.answer: Get out; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. There is a ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here 1R is 1.20, and the low of 44.40 is more than 2R under the 47.20 buy.
questions.lesson_line: First 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, out.

wrong.Hold; 44.40 is now your stop: The first 30-minute low is the new stop, but only up to a ceiling. Past 2R, you are out.
wrong.Wait; the 46.00 stop still rules: The stock is already through it. The gap rule hands the stop to the first 30 minutes.
wrong.Buy more; the price is lower: No adding, and never into a gap against the stop.

questions.story: You bought at 47.20 with the stop at 46.00, so 1R is 1.20. The next morning gaps down to 45.50. The first 30-minute low is 44.40.
questions.simple: Get out, because the first 30-minute low is more than 2R under your buy, and past 2R the rule says exit.

deeper.example: Compare the first 30-minute low with the ceiling. Here 1R is 1.20, so 2R is two of those under the 47.20 buy. The low of 44.40 sits farther down than that, so the ceiling beats the new-stop rule. Had the low been closer to the buy, it would have become the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
the key is a comparison against 2R

questions.q: The open is past your 3R level. Your move?
choices: Take the first third at the open
Wait for 104.82 on a pullback down
Hold it all and trail the average
Sell the whole lot at the open
questions.answer: Take the first third at the open
questions.why: Take the first third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. A third comes off at 3R, another third at 5R, and the last third trails. Here 106.00 is past the 3R level of 104.82. Waiting for a pullback to 104.82 may never come.
questions.lesson_line: Gap past a trim level: take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for 104.82 on a pullback down: You may never see it again. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.
wrong.Hold it all and trail the average: The trail is for the last third, after the trims.
wrong.Sell the whole lot at the open: The plan is a third at 3R, a third at 5R, then the trail.

questions.story: You bought at 101.19 with the stop at 99.98. Your 3R level is 104.82. Two days later the stock opens at 106.00.
questions.simple: A stock that opens past a trim level gets that trim at the open, so sell the first third now.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.5%. Buy 109.42, stop 105.86. How many shares does the stop allow?
questions.why: 140 shares. Risk is 0.5% of 100,000. The stop distance is 109.42 minus 105.86. Divide the risk by that distance and round down to 140. The size is the smaller of that and the 40% position cap. Here 140 shares cost far less than the cap, so the risk size wins. The stop is 3.3% from the buy. We size to the stop and never tighten it.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Wider stop, fewer shares.
questions.simple: The stop distance sets the size, and risk divided by that distance rounds down to 140 shares.

deeper.trap: Do not round the shares up. One more share than the rule allows pushes the loss on a full stop-out past the risk you chose. The rule rounds down so the loss never passes the risk.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the sizing rule is in the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Which average trails a fresh 200-day remount?
choices: The 21-day, for a steadier name
The 3-day, for a fast mover
The 200-day, the line you retook
The 50-day, for any remount
questions.answer: The 21-day, for a steadier name
questions.why: The 21-day, for a steadier name. A fresh 200-day remount is an earlier-stage, steadier name, so the last third trails under the 21-day. A fast mover trails the 10-day. Either way, sell on a close below the average.
questions.lesson_line: Steady name, 21-day. Fast mover, 10-day.

wrong.The 3-day, for a fast mover: That is far too tight and shakes you out of a runner.
wrong.The 200-day, the line you retook: The line you just retook is far too slow to trail.
wrong.The 50-day, for any remount: The card names the 21-day for a steadier name and the 10-day for a fast mover.

questions.simple: A fresh 200-day remount is a steadier name, so it trails the 21-day, while a fast mover trails the 10-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52, adjustable)

questions.q: What now?
choices: Sell it and free the money
Hold; the stop has not been hit
Add to it while the stop holds
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. Here the stock sits at 0.5R with no trim off and the stop not hit, but the time stop still applies. Chop is this setup's main failure.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions, under 1R: out.

wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R, not at 0.5R.
wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit: The stop is not the only exit. A trade still under 1R after 10 sessions is sold.
wrong.Add to it while the stop holds: The plan is one price, one stop, no adds.

questions.story: Ten sessions after the buy, the stock sits at 0.5R. The stop has not been hit and no trim has come off.
questions.simple: Sell it, because a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold to free the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Where do the first two trims come off?
choices: A third at 3R, a third at 5R
Half at 2R and half at 4R
The whole position at 3R
A third each at 1R, 2R and 3R
questions.answer: A third at 3R, a third at 5R
questions.why: A third at 3R and another third at 5R, then trail the last third. The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R. The second third at 5R is the default plan and can be adjusted.
questions.lesson_line: Third at 3R, third at 5R, trail the rest.

wrong.A third each at 1R, 2R and 3R: Trimming that early cuts the runner. The first trim is at 3R.
wrong.Half at 2R and half at 4R: That is not our plan. The hard rule is a third at 3R.
wrong.The whole position at 3R: The last third rides the trail.

questions.simple: Sell a third at 3R and another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, adjustable)

questions.q: Most Remount trades win small, so cut the runner early to lock in the gain.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Expect most trades to lose, and to lose small: the line is retaken, lost again, and the stop takes it within days. The few runners pay for those losses, so do not cut the runner early. Cutting it early removes what carries the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Most lose small. The runners pay for the rest.
questions.simple: False. Most Remount trades lose small, and a few big winners pay for them, so cutting a runner early hurts.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging the setup by its win rate. In the replay behind our card, about 4 in 5 trades hit the first stop within 60 sessions. The few runners pay for those losses. Cut a runner at the first small gain and you lose the few big winners that carry the setup.

reasons: the deeper note cites the replay's 4-in-5 figure, which changes with the data

questions.q: What is your plan from here?
choices: Hold to 5R, then trail the rest
Sell it all now; a win is a win
Widen the stop to give it more room
Add more shares since it is working
questions.answer: Hold to 5R, then trail the rest
questions.why: Hold to 5R, then trail the rest. Most Remount trades lose small: in our replay about 4 in 5 hit the first stop within 60 sessions. The few runners pay for them, so do not cut the runner early. Another third comes off at 5R, then the trail takes the last third. The stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Let the runner run. The trail does the selling.

wrong.Sell it all now; a win is a win: Most trades lose small, so cutting the runner early gives up what pays for the losers.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it more room: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Add more shares since it is working: Full size at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.story: You sold a third at 3R and moved the stop to breakeven. The stock now sits at 4R, above its 10-day, and you want to cash out.
questions.simple: Keep holding, because the few big winners pay for the many small losses, and the trail does the selling.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52)
the replay figure comes from a dated run

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Only on a new trigger, as a new trade
Yes, it is the same setup
Yes, with a wider stop
Yes, at double size
questions.answer: Only on a new trigger, as a new trade
questions.why: Only on a new trigger. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop, at most 3 a week and 6 a month on one stock.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a signal. Wait for a new trigger.

wrong.Yes, it is the same setup: The same setup is not a trigger. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: A wider stop to get back in is the mistake, not the fix.
wrong.Yes, at double size: Doubling to win it back makes a small loss bigger.

questions.story: Your first Remount stopped out. Four sessions later the stock closes back over the 200-day again.

questions.q: Remounts do best while the index sits under its own 200-day.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Remounts are best after a correction, as the indexes remount their own lines and leaders remount first. They are weak with the index under its own 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: The best Remounts come as the market itself turns up.
questions.simple: False. Remounts do best after a correction, as the indexes retake their own lines, and are weak with the index under its 200-day.

deeper.trap: Weak is a read, not a ban. The card calls a remount weak with the index under its own 200-day. The trigger, the stop and the size rules stay the same, and the 200-day rule for the stock itself is still hard.

reasons: the index-under-its-200-day line is proposed on card 32 and held (D-023)

questions.q: On a Red market reading we are mostly in cash, so a textbook Remount waits.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Red means mostly cash and shorts, and the Remount card says Red allows no new longs. A Remount is a long, so it waits. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Orange allows only A+ setups.
questions.lesson_line: Red means mostly cash. The setup waits.
questions.simple: True. On a Red reading we hold mostly cash, and the card says no new longs, so a Remount waits.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, D46)

questions.q: Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the line is a chop line
Pass; the candle is too weak
Take it; it closed well above
Take it, but at half the size
questions.answer: Pass; the line is a chop line
questions.why: Pass. A flat line that price has crossed back and forth for weeks is a chop line. Buying its reclaim is a listed mistake. Whipsaw is the main miss. ChartSchool says crossover signals are less reliable in sideways markets. Weinstein's stage work says to avoid trading a sideways chop with no defined trend.
questions.lesson_line: A flat line crossed for weeks is a chop line. Pass.

wrong.Pass; the candle is too weak: The candle is strong. The flat line that price keeps crossing is the problem.
wrong.Take it; it closed well above: A close above a line it has crossed for weeks proves little. Whipsaw is the main miss.
wrong.Take it, but at half the size: Half size on a chop line is still a chop trade.

questions.story: A stock has crossed back and forth over its flat 200-day for weeks. Today it closes well above the line on a strong green candle.
questions.simple: Pass, because a flat line that price keeps crossing is a chop line, and buying its retake is a known mistake.

reasons: the chop count is held (D-075) and is never keyed

questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: The one that clears every average
The one with the 50-day overhead
Both grade the same; each is a pass
The one with the tighter stop
questions.answer: The one that clears every average
questions.why: The one that clears every average. Clearing all the averages at once is an A plus cue. Leaving the 50-day overhead and falling is a B minus cue. These are cues, not a fixed score. The grade sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Clear every average at once. That is the A plus picture.

wrong.The one with the 50-day overhead: Leaving the 50-day overhead and falling is a B minus cue.
wrong.Both grade the same; each is a pass: Clearing every average at once is an A plus cue; a falling average overhead is not.
wrong.The one with the tighter stop: The story gives no stops. Our card's grade cues are about the averages, not the stop width.

questions.story: Two remounts of the 200-day. One also clears the 20 and 50-day at once. The other leaves the 50-day overhead and falling.
questions.simple: Clearing every average at once is an A plus cue, and a falling 50-day overhead is a B minus cue.

reasons: +2 grading is discretionary in the account rulebook (E50)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What is the call?
choices: Pass; the retake lacks real buying
Pass; it was under too briefly
Buy; the line is retaken on the close
Buy half size and use a tight stop
questions.answer: Pass; the retake lacks real buying
questions.why: Pass. The stock lost its 50-day on heavy volume and came back on light volume. Our card lists that light-volume reclaim after a heavy-volume break as an invalidation. Few buyers came with the close, and IBD notes stocks often need a large boost of buying power to muscle back above a lost 50-day line.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy break, light retake: no trade.

wrong.Buy; the line is retaken on the close: The line is retaken, but a light-volume reclaim after a heavy-volume break is an invalidation.
wrong.Buy half size and use a tight stop: Half size does not fix it. A light retake after a heavy break is no trade.
wrong.Pass; it was under too briefly: Three weeks under the line is long enough to count as lost. The problem is light buying after a heavy break.

questions.story: A stock lost its 50-day on heavy volume and stayed under it for three weeks. It drifts back over the line and closes above it on light volume.
questions.simple: Pass. The break came on heavy volume and the retake on light volume, so too few buyers came back to trust the line.

deeper.trap: Heavy volume on the break and light volume on the retake is the pattern to fear. The close is back over the line, but few buyers came with it. A close over the line alone does not make a Remount.

reasons: the volume rule is proposed on card 13 and held (D-006)

questions.q: Remount or U&R?
choices: A U&R, back within 3 sessions
A Remount of the base low
An Oops, a one-session undercut
A breakdown to sell, not a buy
questions.answer: A U&R, back within 3 sessions
questions.why: A U&R. Our card says a U&R closes back above the level within 3 sessions of the undercut. It is bought as the level is retaken. Here the stock was back over its base low by Thursday. A Remount needs the line lost for real.
questions.lesson_line: Back in 3 sessions: a U&R. A long stay under the line: a Remount.

wrong.A Remount of the base low: A Remount lost the line for real. This was two closes under, a short dip.
wrong.An Oops, a one-session undercut: An Oops is one session. This took closes on two days under the low.
wrong.A breakdown to sell, not a buy: It closed back over the low within 3 sessions. That undercut is bought as the level is retaken.

questions.story: The stock closed under its base low on Tuesday and Wednesday. It closed back over it on Thursday.
questions.simple: It closed back over the base low within 3 sessions, so it is a U&R and not a Remount.

deeper.trap: Both setups end with a close back over a line, so that close does not name the setup. Count the closes under the line. Two is a dip. A Remount needs the line lost for real.

reasons: +2 the border with the Remount is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: An Oops; a one-day reversal
A Remount of the 50-day line
A Remount of a lost price level
An AVWAP reclaim after an event
questions.answer: An Oops; a one-day reversal
questions.why: An Oops. It is one session. It opens under the prior close, trades under the prior day's low and closes back over the prior close. A Remount needs a line lost for real, which takes more than one session.
questions.lesson_line: One session is an Oops. A lost line takes days.

wrong.A Remount of the 50-day line: No 50-day is in the story. A Remount follows a line lost for real, and one session cannot do that.
wrong.A Remount of a lost price level: No level was lost over days here. A Remount needs a line lost for real.
wrong.An AVWAP reclaim after an event: No event day or volume-bent line is in the story.

questions.story: Monday closed at 40.00 after a low of 39.50. Tuesday opens at 39.20 and trades down to 39.00. It then closes at 40.30.
questions.simple: One session that opens under the prior close and closes back over it is an Oops, not a Remount.

deeper.trap: An Oops and a Remount both end with a close back above something. Check the line. An Oops needs only the prior day's low and prior close, all in one session. A Remount needs a line the stock really lost, an average or a held level.

reasons: +2 the border with the Remount is a held decision (D-074)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Which form is this?
choices: The level form of a Remount
A 50-day or 200-day Remount
A U&R of the 100.00 price
An AVWAP reclaim from a date
questions.answer: The level form of a Remount
questions.why: The level form of a Remount. A horizontal level that held before it broke, then lost and retaken, is the level form. It is not the moving-average form, because the line is not the 50-day or the 200-day. It is not a U&R, which closes back above within 3 sessions. It is not an AVWAP, which starts at one event day and bends with volume.
questions.lesson_line: Flat level that held, lost, retaken: the level form.

wrong.A 50-day or 200-day Remount: The line is a flat price, not the 50-day or the 200-day.
wrong.A U&R of the 100.00 price: Three weeks under the line is far past a U&R.
wrong.An AVWAP reclaim from a date: A flat price is not an AVWAP. The AVWAP bends with volume from an event day.

questions.story: A stock broke out above 100.00 and held it for months. Later it closed under 100.00 and stayed there for three weeks. Today it closes back above.
questions.simple: It is the level form, because the line is a flat price level that held before it broke and was then retaken.

deeper.counter: Not every flat price is a level. The card wants it to have held first: at least 10 of the 15 closes before the break at or above it. A price the stock chopped through for weeks does not qualify, and buying it is a listed mistake.

reasons: the lines that count and the time under the line are held (D-073, D-074)

questions.q: How do you read this close?
choices: A marginal poke, no remount yet
A clear remount, pause comes next
A U&R, a quick snap back over
An Oops, a one-session undercut
questions.answer: A marginal poke, no remount yet
questions.why: A marginal poke. A close 0.08 ATR over the line is inside the noise, so ESS could not be called a remount that evening. Wait for the clear close. ESS remounted clearly in the next sessions and reached 14.9R.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the clear close. A poke is not a retake.

wrong.A clear remount, pause comes next: A close that small over the line is a marginal poke inside the noise, not a clear retake.
wrong.A U&R, a quick snap back over: A U&R is back above within 3 sessions. This stock sat under the line for weeks.
wrong.An Oops, a one-session undercut: An Oops is one session. This stock sat under the line for weeks.

questions.story: After weeks under the 50-day, the stock closes just 0.08 ATR over it, a small slice of a normal day's range. Nothing else is wrong.
questions.simple: A close only 0.08 ATR over the line is a poke inside the noise, so wait for a clear close.

deeper.trap: Waiting did not cost the move here. ESS remounted clearly a few sessions later and reached 14.9R. The mistake is buying the poke itself. Buying before the close is above the line, or on a marginal poke a few cents over it, is a listed mistake.

reasons: the remount-day margin is proposed and held (D-075)

questions.q: Your move before the buy?
choices: Nothing; wait for a new close
Buy anyway; it is just one close
Buy half size, stop at the low
Nothing; the setup is dead for good
questions.answer: Nothing; wait for a new close
questions.why: Nothing. A close back under the line before the trigger means no trade. The remount is off until it closes above the line again. The earlier close above the line does not count once the line is lost again. Buying anyway, at any size, is buying a failed retake.
questions.lesson_line: Back under the line before the buy means no trade.

wrong.Buy anyway; it is just one close: A close back under the line before the trigger means no trade.
wrong.Buy half size, stop at the low: Half size does not fix a failed retake.
wrong.Nothing; the setup is dead for good: The remount is off until it closes above the line again. It is not off for good.

questions.story: The stock remounted its 200-day yesterday. Today, before you buy, it closes back under the line.
questions.simple: Do nothing. A close back under the line before you buy cancels the retake, so wait for a new close above it.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding on to the earlier close above the line. Once the stock closes back under it before your trigger, the retake is off. It is on again only after the stock closes above the line again. Until then you have no trade, and no size makes it one.

questions.q: Do you buy?
choices: Pass; the gap is too far past 50.00
Pass; the trigger has not fired yet
Buy; price traded over the high
Buy with a wider stop to fit the gap
questions.answer: Pass; the gap is too far past 50.00
questions.why: Pass. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. The quiet day's high of 50.00 is the buy point, and a fill at 52.60 is more than 4% above it. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the buy point and I am done.

wrong.Buy with a wider stop to fit the gap: A wider stop to fit a late fill is the mistake, not the fix.
wrong.Pass; the trigger has not fired yet: The trigger did fire, since the stock opened over 50.00. The problem is the fill, not the signal.
wrong.Buy; price traded over the high: It did trade over the high, but the fill is more than 4% over the buy point. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

questions.story: The quiet day's high is 50.00. The stock gaps up to 52.60 at the open.
questions.simple: Pass, because the gap puts the fill more than 4% above the buy point, and we never chase past 4%.

deeper.trap: The trigger did fire, since price traded over the high. The 4% check is made on the fill, not on the signal. A gap up is where it bites. The stop stays under the buy point, so the risk per share grows and the share count has to shrink.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
the key needs a percent check
which buy point counts is held (D-022)
edited at the cold check

questions.q: Do you buy?
choices: Pass; it is too stretched to buy
Pass; the trigger has not fired yet
Buy; the trigger fired over the high
Buy, and plan to trim a third at 3R
questions.answer: Pass; it is too stretched to buy
questions.why: Pass. Skip a stock that is more than 10% over its 10-day average. A stock that far above its short average is too stretched to buy. The trigger firing over the high does not lift that rule.
questions.lesson_line: More than ten percent over the 10-day: skip.

wrong.Buy; the trigger fired over the high: The trigger fired, and the stretch rule still says no.
wrong.Pass; the trigger has not fired yet: The stock traded over the quiet day's high, so the trigger did fire. The stretch rule is the reason to pass.
wrong.Buy, and plan to trim a third at 3R: A trim plan does not fix a stretched entry. The stretch check comes before the order.

questions.story: The quiet day holds above the line. The next morning the stock trades over its high and sits 12% over its 10-day average.
questions.simple: Pass, because the stock is 12% over its 10-day average and we skip a long more than 10% over it.

deeper.trap: All the other rules can line up and this one still says skip. The Remount line, the quiet day and the trigger can be perfect. The stretch check looks at the distance from the 10-day average. Run it before you place the order, not after the fill.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
edited at the cold check

questions.q: Do you buy?
choices: No; the report comes tonight
No; the trigger has not fired
Yes; the trigger just fired
Yes, at half the usual size
questions.answer: No; the report comes tonight
questions.why: No. We take no new buy in the 3 sessions before a report, and this report is tonight. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. After the report, a remount on the reaction day itself is allowed.
questions.lesson_line: Report tonight, no buy. After the report, it can trigger.

wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Half size is still a new buy inside the window.
wrong.No; the trigger has not fired: The trigger did fire, since price trades over the quiet day's high. The report is the reason to pass.
wrong.Yes; the trigger just fired: The trigger fired, but we make no new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.

questions.story: A textbook 200-day remount has had its quiet inside day. This morning price trades over that day's high. The company reports earnings tonight.
questions.simple: No, because the report is tonight and we make no new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.

deeper.trap: Report timing cuts both ways. Tonight's report blocks the buy. Once it is out, a remount on the reaction day itself is allowed. AMD remounted its 50-day the day after a report that came after the close on 2023-10-31. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: You grade it B minus. How do you size it?
choices: Smaller than a normal B setup
The same as a normal B setup
Larger than a normal B setup
No trade; a B minus is barred
questions.answer: Smaller than a normal B setup
questions.why: Smaller. Setup grades set the size: A and B at normal size, A+ sized up, B minus or lower sized down.
questions.lesson_line: B minus or lower is sized down, not skipped.

wrong.The same as a normal B setup: Only A and B setups get normal size. B minus or lower is sized down.
wrong.Larger than a normal B setup: Only an A+ is sized up. B minus is sized down.
wrong.No trade; a B minus is barred: A lower grade is not a ban. B minus or lower is sized down, not skipped.

questions.story: A stock fell 25% over months but never closed under its 200-day. Today it remounts its 50-day for the first time. The 50-day is still curling lower.
questions.simple: A B minus is sized down, so the position is smaller than a normal B setup.

deeper.trap: A weak cue lowers the grade but does not ban the trade. The grade sets the size, so a B minus is sized down.

reasons: +2 grade and size rest on the account rulebook (D38, E50)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What does that add?
choices: A point toward a higher grade
A warning: it is ahead of the market
Nothing; the index does not matter
An automatic A plus on its own
questions.answer: A point toward a higher grade
questions.why: A point toward a higher grade. A leader that lost the line in a market shakeout and remounted before the index did is an A plus cue. Leaders remount first after a correction, as the indexes remount their own lines. The cue is one input. It does not replace the 200-day rule, the quiet-day trigger or the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders remount first. That is a cue toward A plus.

wrong.A warning: it is ahead of the market: Leaders remount first. That is a cue, not a warning.
wrong.Nothing; the index does not matter: The market matters. A leader remounting first is a grade cue.
wrong.An automatic A plus on its own: Grading is a judgment call. The cue lifts the grade; it does not set it.

questions.story: A leader lost its 50-day in a market shakeout. It remounts while the index is still under its own 50-day, though above its own 200-day.
questions.simple: It is an A plus cue: a leader that lost its line in a shakeout and retook it before the index did.

deeper.trap: The cue lifts the grade, not the rules. The remount still needs a close above the 200-day, a quiet day above the line and a real stop. Grading is a judgment call, so treat the cue as one input, not a checklist.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E50: grading is a judgment call)

questions.q: Where does that leave you?
choices: Nothing; wait for a fresh trigger
Buy back at 59.54; the line held
Buy now and skip the stop this time
Widen the stop on the next try
questions.answer: Nothing; wait for a fresh trigger
questions.why: Nothing. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop. It is limited to 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. DOCU gapped under its stop on 2024-03-15, then held the 50-day for the next 20 sessions and traded up to 61.47. The level was right; the trigger did not run.
questions.lesson_line: Right level, wrong trigger. Wait for a new one.

wrong.Buy back at 59.54; the line held: The line held, but the trigger is gone. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger.
wrong.Widen the stop on the next try: The stop sits under the low it marks. Widening it only makes the loss bigger.

questions.story: You bought at 59.54 with the stop at 58.44. A gap under the stop the next morning ended it. The stock then held its 50-day for 20 sessions.
questions.simple: Do nothing now. A second try needs a fresh trigger and its own stop, even when the line held.

deeper.trap: Hindsight makes the stop look wrong, but the stop did its job. DOCU gapped under 58.44 the next morning and the trade ended there. A right level is not a right trade: the stock reached only +1.75R inside the window, short of the 3R trim.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)

questions.q: What does this teach?
choices: The stop was the cost of the setup
Widen the stop after the buy to ride it
Never use stops on 200-day names
Buy back at 206.55 on a pullback
questions.answer: The stop was the cost of the setup
questions.why: The stop was the cost of the setup. FDX was bought at 198.12 with the stop at 195.31. The next day's low was 193.94, so the stop took it. Later it reached the 3R level, 206.55, without us. That was a shakeout. A stop-out that later turns around is still a planned loss, and most tries lose small.
questions.lesson_line: Some stops are shakeouts. That is the price of the setup.

wrong.Never use stops on 200-day names: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
wrong.Buy back at 206.55 on a pullback: A new try needs its own trigger and its own stop, not a price from the old trade.
wrong.Widen the stop after the buy to ride it: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.story: You bought a 200-day remount at 198.12 with the stop at 195.31. It stopped you out the next day. Weeks later it reached your old 3R level, 206.55.
questions.simple: A stop-out that later turns around is the normal cost of the setup, not proof that the stop was wrong.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a stop by what the stock does after it. FDX stopped out on a low of 193.94, then reached 206.55 weeks later. The stop did its job. Buying back later is a new try, and a new try needs its own trigger and its own stop.

questions.q: How do you read this loss?
choices: The index was weak, so the remount was
Bad luck; nothing in the chart showed it
The stop was too tight for this stock
A flaw in the 200-day line itself
questions.answer: The index was weak, so the remount was
questions.why: The index was weak, so the remount was. A remount is weak with the index under its own 200-day. AAPL opened lower and traded through the stop the next day. The stop did its job, and most tries lose small.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart is weak when the index is weak.

wrong.A flaw in the 200-day line itself: The story points at the market, not the line: the index sat under its own 200-day.
wrong.Bad luck; nothing in the chart showed it: The story shows a clue: the S&P 500 sat under its own 200-day, and a remount is weak then.
wrong.The stop was too tight for this stock: The stop never goes wider. It was the exit, and it did its job.

questions.story: A 200-day remount example. The buy was 163.43 with the stop at 159.25. The S&P 500 sat under its own 200-day. Next day it opened at 159.90 and traded through the stop.
questions.simple: The index sat under its own 200-day, so the remount was weak and the stop did its job.

deeper.trap: One loss does not prove the setup or the stop was wrong. Most tries lose small. A weak index makes a weak remount, and the stop did its job.

reasons: +2 index under its own 200-day as a hard line is a held decision (D-023)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What did the heavy volume do for the trade?
choices: It did not offset the weak index
It turned this into an A plus setup
It made the stop matter much less
It made strong follow-through likely
questions.answer: It did not offset the weak index
questions.why: It did not offset the weak index. A remount is weak with the index under its own 200-day. PYPL remounted its 200-day on 2.98x volume, the earnings reaction, in the October 2018 correction. SPY was under its own 200-day, and the stock was stopped the next session. One example is not a law.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume does not save a remount in a weak market.

wrong.It turned this into an A plus setup: A remount is weak with the index under its own 200-day. PYPL had heavy volume and still stopped out.
wrong.It made the stop matter much less: The stop is never optional. PYPL's stop is what ended the trade.
wrong.It made strong follow-through likely: PYPL had heavy volume and was stopped out the next session.

questions.story: A 200-day remount shows heavy volume on the earnings reaction day. The index sits under its own 200-day and is making new lows. You buy over the quiet day's high.
questions.simple: Heavy volume did not save it, because a remount is weak when the index sits under its 200-day.

deeper.trap: A buy over the quiet day's high is a trigger, not a promise. The same heavy volume that excites a chart can still meet a falling index. Check the index against its own 200-day before you trust a remount.

reasons: the key rests on one dossier example
the index line is proposed and held (D-023)
the old key said Nothing and was softened

questions.q: Which one do you buy?
choices: A, the leader chart
B, the 50-day retake
C, the flat-line close
None; wait for better
questions.answer: A, the leader chart
questions.why: A. It clears every average, sits above the 200-day, has a stop inside about 3% and a Green reading. B is a 50-day retake with the close under a falling 200-day. We take no longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long. C is a flat line crossed back and forth, a chop line and a listed mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Context first: above the 200-day, not a chop line, stop inside 3%.

wrong.B, the 50-day retake: The close is still under a falling 200-day. We take no longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long.
wrong.C, the flat-line close: A flat line crossed ten times is a chop line.
wrong.None; wait for better: Chart A meets every rule here, so there is a trade to take.

questions.story: Three charts. A: a leader clears every average, with a quiet day, a 2% stop and a Green reading. B: the 50-day retaken, with the close still under a falling 200-day. C: a flat 200-day crossed ten times in 60 sessions.
questions.simple: Buy A, since B is under the 200-day and C is a chop line, while A passes every check.

deeper.counter: Check the 200-day first. B fails it. C may close over its line, but a flat line crossed ten times is not a floor. Only A has the line, the quiet day, a stop inside about 3% and the market on its side.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, A13, F65)
the A plus cue touches E50

questions.q: Hidden ticker, after a dip under its 50-day. Read the last two days. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; the quiet day holds the line
Pass; the close sits under the 50-day
Pass; the remount close was marginal
Take it; buy now, before the high breaks
questions.answer: Take it; the quiet day holds the line
questions.why: Take it. The remount close was strong, +1.3 ATR over the 50-day. The next day was an inside day that held above the line. That quiet day arms the buy: a market order as price trades over its high, stop a few cents under its low. In this example the buy came the next session and 3R the day after. It is one example, and most tries lose small.
questions.lesson_line: Strong retake, quiet day above the line: that is the trade.

wrong.Pass; the close sits under the 50-day: Look again: the quiet day closes above the 50-day.
wrong.Pass; the remount close was marginal: The remount close was strong, +1.3 ATR over the line, well clear of it.
wrong.Take it; buy now, before the high breaks: The buy is a market order as price trades over the quiet day's high, not before it. Buying early is anticipating the trigger.

questions.simple: Take it. The close was a strong retake of the 50-day, and the quiet day after it held above the line.

deeper.example: NKE spent 7 days under its 50-day after the 2020 recovery. The close on 2020-08-05 was a strong retake. The next day was an inside day. The buy came on 2020-08-07 at 101.19 with the stop at 99.98, 1.2% away, and 3R came the session after the buy.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the pause entry over a quiet inside day)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day it closes back over the 50-day. Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the close is under the 200-day
Take it; the 50-day was just retaken
Take it; the 50-day is above the 200-day
Pass; the 50-day is only a minor line
questions.answer: Pass; the close is under the 200-day
questions.why: Pass. The reclaim close was 274.51, under the 200-day SMA at 295.88. A 50-day reclaim counts only with the close above the 200-day too. We do not buy a Remount below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A fifty-day retake under the 200-day is not a buy.

wrong.Take it; the 50-day was just retaken: A 50-day reclaim counts only with the close above the 200-day too.
wrong.Take it; the 50-day is above the 200-day: Here the 50-day sits under the 200-day, and so does the close.
wrong.Pass; the 50-day is only a minor line: The 50-day matters to many traders. The block here is the 200-day.

questions.simple: Pass, because the close of 274.51 is under the 200-day at 295.88, and we do not buy a Remount below it.

deeper.trap: A 50-day retake looks like a Remount, but the 200-day test comes first. Here 274.51 sat under 295.88, so the close failed it.

reasons: +2 no longs below the 200-day is in the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: A clean setup lets us own up to 5% of a stock's average daily volume.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, however clean the setup. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Never more than 1% of daily volume.
questions.simple: False, because we never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only
+2 rests on the account rulebook

questions.q: By our default, after the first third comes off at 3R, where does the stop go?
choices: Up to breakeven, our entry price
Up halfway between stop and entry
Up to 2R to lock in some profit
Up to the 10-day average at once
questions.answer: Up to breakeven, our entry price
questions.why: Up to breakeven, our entry price. Our rules put the stop at breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R. Our card makes it the first trim by default. So after the third comes off at 3R, the stop goes to entry. It only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: First trim off, stop to breakeven.

wrong.Up halfway between stop and entry: A halfway stop is not in the plan. The stop goes to breakeven, our entry.
wrong.Up to 2R to lock in some profit: The plan moves the stop to breakeven, our entry, not into profit.
wrong.Up to the 10-day average at once: The 10-day trail is for the last third, after the 5R trim.

questions.simple: After the first third sells at 3R, the stop moves up to our entry. That is breakeven.

deeper.counter: Our rules allow the breakeven move anywhere from 2R to 5R, so moving earlier than the first trim is allowed. Moving the stop down never is.

reasons: +2 rests on the account rulebook (B19)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell a third; the stop goes to breakeven
Sell half; the stop stays
Hold it all; the stop stays
Sell it all
questions.answer: Sell a third; the stop goes to breakeven
questions.why: Sell a third; the stop goes to breakeven. The hard rule is a third at 3R, and the stop moves to breakeven at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: Third off at 3R, stop to breakeven.

wrong.Sell half; the stop stays: The hard rule is a third at 3R. The stop moves to breakeven at the first trim by default.
wrong.Hold it all; the stop stays: The first third comes off at 3R. Holding it all skips the plan.
wrong.Sell it all: The last third rides the trail. Another third comes off at 5R.

questions.story: You bought at 101.19 with the stop at 99.98. The stock trades to 104.82, which is 3R.

questions.q: In Wyckoff's method, what is a shakeout meant to do to holders?
choices: Get them to sell to large operators
Lock them in so they ride a rally
Raise the volume for a later breakout
Prove the downtrend is here to stay
questions.answer: Get them to sell to large operators
questions.why: Get them to sell to large operators. In Wyckoff's method, a shakeout is a rapid drop meant to induce holders in long positions to sell to large operators. Morales and Kacher describe a related picture on a line: the stock undercuts it, fakes out sellers, then rallies back above it.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is a drop meant to make holders sell to large operators.

wrong.Lock them in so they ride a rally: A shakeout is meant to get holders out, not lock them in.
wrong.Raise the volume for a later breakout: In Wyckoff's description the aim is to induce selling, not to raise volume.
wrong.Prove the downtrend is here to stay: In Wyckoff's picture the drop is meant to get holders out once an advance has started. It does not prove a downtrend.

questions.simple: A shakeout is a sharp drop meant to get holders to sell their shares to large operators.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; Orange allows only A plus
Take it at full size, like Green
Take it at smaller size, like Yellow
Pass; Orange means no new trades
questions.answer: Pass; Orange allows only A plus
questions.why: Pass. Orange allows only an A+ remount, and this one is a B, so it waits. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. The reading is a guide, not a hard cap, but in Orange the guide says A plus only.
questions.lesson_line: Orange means A plus only. A B waits.

wrong.Take it at full size, like Green: Full risk is the Green reading. Orange allows only A+ setups.
wrong.Take it at smaller size, like Yellow: Smaller and fewer is the Yellow reading. Orange allows only A+ setups, and this one is a B.
wrong.Pass; Orange means no new trades: Orange is not Red. It still allows A+ setups. Red is mostly cash and shorts.

questions.story: The market reading is Orange. A Remount sets up cleanly, but you grade it a B.
questions.simple: Pass. In an Orange market only A plus setups are taken, and this one is a B.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating Orange as a smaller Yellow. Yellow lowers the size and the number of positions. Orange raises the grade we demand: only A+. A B that could be taken in Yellow at a smaller size waits in Orange. The readings are a guide, not a hard cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, the market reading)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Hold; the stop is still the exit
Sell at the close; the line failed
Raise the stop to breakeven, 46.01
Add more shares on the next dip
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. Our card holds a 200-day remount that slips back under the line but stays above the stop. The stop is the exit, and a close back under the line is not an extra exit. This trade closed at 45.60, under the line but above the 44.80 stop. The time stop still applies: a trade under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.lesson_line: Slipped under the line, still above the stop: hold.

wrong.Sell at the close; the line failed: A close back under the line is not an extra exit. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Raise the stop to breakeven, 46.01: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R. The stop stays at 44.80 and only moves up with the plan.
wrong.Add more shares on the next dip: Full size at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.story: You bought a 200-day remount at 46.01 with the stop at 44.80. Three days later it closes at 45.60, back under the 200-day, above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold. A close under the line is not an exit, because the stop is the exit and price is still above it.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating a close under the line as a second stop. That would put two exits on one trade, and they could disagree. The plan has one exit, the stop, plus the time stop for a trade stuck under 1R after 10 trading days. A close under the line is a warning to watch, nothing more.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-008, what a close back under the line means after the buy)

questions.q: Which grades highest?
choices: B; leader first, all averages clear
A; it finally turned after a long fall
C; it retook the 50-day, rest overhead
They all grade about the same
questions.answer: B; leader first, all averages clear
questions.why: B. A leader that remounts before the index is an A plus cue, and so is clearing all the averages at once. A is a first attempt after a long decline and C leaves the averages overhead and falling, so both are B minus cues. These are cues, not a score.
questions.lesson_line: Leader first, every average cleared: that is the A plus picture.

wrong.A; it finally turned after a long fall: A first attempt after a long decline, or a line still curling lower, is a B minus cue.
wrong.C; it retook the 50-day, rest overhead: A retake that leaves averages overhead and falling is a B minus cue.
wrong.They all grade about the same: Grade follows the cues, and these are far apart.

questions.story: Three remounts. A: a first try after a long decline, the line still curling lower. B: a leader that remounts before the index and clears every average. C: the 50-day retaken, other averages overhead and falling.
questions.simple: B grades highest. A leader that remounts before the index and clears every average is the strongest picture, while A and C are weaker.

deeper.trap: The trap is adding up cues like a checklist. A cue is a hint about how much to like a setup, not a score. Here B shows two A plus cues, and A and C each show a B minus cue. The card lists cues. It does not hand out a grade.

reasons: grade cues sit against rulebook E50, which says grading is discretionary

questions.q: The line is 62.00. The deepest close under it was 60.50. ATR, the typical daily move, is 1.20. How many ATR under the line?
questions.why: 1.25 ATR. Take the line minus the deepest close, 62.00 minus 60.50. Divide that by the ATR, 1.20, to get 1.25 ATR. Our card proposes a close at least 0.5 ATR under the line, so this break left the line.
questions.lesson_line: Our card proposes a close at least half an ATR under the line.
questions.simple: Take the gap under the line and divide it by the ATR of 1.20, which gives 1.25 ATR.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only
+2 computed key

questions.q: Our card wants one close 0.5 ATR or more under the line. Did this break leave the line?
choices: No; the dip was too shallow to count
Yes; any close under the line is a break
Yes; the close back over proves it
No; it needs a close under the 200-day
questions.answer: No; the dip was too shallow to count
questions.why: No. Our card asks that at least one close sat 0.5 ATR or more under the line. This dip reached only 0.2 ATR, too shallow to count as a lost line. The close back over is a retake, but there was no real loss to retake.
questions.lesson_line: A dip inside the noise is not a lost line. Wait for a real break.

wrong.Yes; any close under the line is a break: One close under the line is not enough. Our card wants one at least 0.5 ATR under it.
wrong.Yes; the close back over proves it: The close back over is the retake. The break must be deep enough first.
wrong.No; it needs a close under the 200-day: The 200-day is a separate test. This one is about how deep the dip went under the 50-day.

questions.story: A stock held its 50-day for months. It dipped under on a few closes, the deepest only 0.2 ATR below the line. Today it closes back over.
questions.simple: No. A lost line needs one close at least 0.5 ATR under it, and this dip reached only 0.2 ATR.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling any close under a line a break. Our card asks that at least one close sit 0.5 ATR or more under it. A shallow dip inside the noise leaves the line standing, so there is no lost line to retake.

reasons: the 0.5 ATR depth is a threshold on our card that may change

questions.q: A price level counts as a Remount line only if the stock held it before the break.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card proposes that a level must have held before it broke. At least 10 of the 15 closes before the break sit at or above it. A level the stock chopped through for weeks does not count.
questions.lesson_line: A level has to hold before it can be lost.
questions.simple: A level counts only if it held before the break, with at least 10 of 15 closes at or above it.

reasons: +3 one cited fact carries the key
+2 the 10 of 15 count is a proposed card number
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Is 80.00 a real level for a Remount?
choices: No; too few closes were above it
Yes; the retake is what counts
Yes; any round number is a level
No; a Remount uses averages only
questions.answer: No; too few closes were above it
questions.why: No. Our card wants a level that held before it broke. That means at least 10 of the 15 closes before the break were at or above it. Here only 5 did, so 80.00 was a price the stock chopped through, not a level. The level form is real, but the level has to have held first.
questions.lesson_line: Chopping through a price for weeks does not make it a level.

wrong.Yes; the retake is what counts: The retake comes second. The level has to have held before the break.
wrong.Yes; any round number is a level: A round number counts only if it held. Weeks of chop through it says it did not.
wrong.No; a Remount uses averages only: The level form is real. A price level that held before it broke counts.

questions.story: A stock breaks under 80.00 and later closes back over it. In the 15 sessions before the break, only 5 closes were at or above 80.00. It had chopped through that price for weeks.
questions.simple: No. A level has to hold before it breaks, and this price was chopped through for weeks, so it did not hold.

reasons: the 10 of 15 closes line is a threshold on our card that may change

questions.q: What is our card's variant buy?
choices: Buy as it turns positive on the day
Buy the open to catch the dip
Wait for a close over the prior high
Skip it; a gap down ends the setup
questions.answer: Buy as it turns positive on the day
questions.why: Buy as it turns positive on the day. A gap down that stays above the line is the case for this variant. Our card buys when price turns positive on the day, at market, with the stop a few cents under that day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Gap down, line held: buy the turn to positive.

wrong.Buy the open to catch the dip: The variant waits for price to turn positive on the day, so it does not buy the open.
wrong.Wait for a close over the prior high: That waits for the daily close. This variant buys the turn on the day itself.
wrong.Skip it; a gap down ends the setup: A gap down that stays above the line is the case this variant is for.

questions.story: Yesterday was a clean remount day. Today the stock gaps down at the open but stays above the line. You have not bought yet.
questions.simple: On a gap down that holds the line, we buy as price turns positive, with the stop under that day's low.

reasons: +2 the stop and market entry rest on the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: A Remount can be timed on the hourly chart, on a higher low or a flag.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card teaches the hourly timing, a higher low or a flag, as a variant. Daily drills cannot show it. The daily rules stay the base: the close above the line and above the 200-day still come first.
questions.lesson_line: Hourly timing is a variant. The daily rules stay the base.
questions.simple: True, our card teaches hourly timing as a variant, but the daily rules stay the base.

deeper.trap: Hourly timing refines the entry. It does not replace the tests. Do not buy under the line because an hourly bar looks good. The close above the line comes first.

reasons: +3 one card line carries the key

questions.q: Do you add to the position?
choices: No; one price, one stop, no adds
Yes; add half with the same stop
Yes; add, and move the stop to average
No; sell half to lock in the gain
questions.answer: No; one price, one stop, no adds
questions.why: No. The plan is the full size at one price with one stop, and no adding. Our card teaches one entry per trade. A trade that works is held and trimmed, a third at 3R and another third at 5R, not added to.
questions.lesson_line: One entry, one price, one stop. Liking it more is not a trigger.

wrong.Yes; add half with the same stop: Half now and half later is two entries. We buy the full size at one price.
wrong.Yes; add, and move the stop to average: Moving the stop to fit an add breaks the one-stop rule.
wrong.No; sell half to lock in the gain: Trims come at 3R and 5R, a third each. Half now is not the plan.

questions.story: You bought a Remount at 40.00 with the stop at 38.80. Two days later it holds above the line again. You like it even more.
questions.simple: No. We buy the full size once, at one price with one stop, and liking a trade more is not a reason to add.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, the full size at one price with one stop, no adding)

questions.q: Bought at 59.54 with the stop at 58.44. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 65.04. One R is the fill minus the stop. Five R is five of those. Add them to the fill, 59.54, to get 65.04. By default the second third comes off there.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 5R before the open. The second third comes off there.
questions.simple: Five times the risk per share, added to the 59.54 fill, gives 65.04.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the third at 5R is a rulebook rule

questions.q: By our default plan, what comes off at 5R?
choices: Another 100; trail the last 100
The other 200; no trail needed
Another 50; trail the other 150
Nothing; wait for the 21-day
questions.answer: Another 100; trail the last 100
questions.why: Another 100, a third of the position. After the first third at 3R comes another third at 5R, then you trail the last third. You bought 300 shares and sold 100 at 3R, so 100 more come off at 5R and 100 ride the trail. The plan is adjustable, but this is the default.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, then the trail.

wrong.The other 200; no trail needed: The plan keeps the last third on the trail. A third comes off at 5R, not all of it.
wrong.Another 50; trail the other 150: Half a third is not the plan. The second trim is a third of the position.
wrong.Nothing; wait for the 21-day: The trail is for the last third, after both trims. At 5R the second third comes off.

questions.story: You bought 300 shares of a Remount and sold 100 at 3R. 200 shares remain. Today the stock reaches 5R.
questions.simple: Sell another 100, a third of the 300 shares, and trail the last 100.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, adjustable)
the key is computed from the share counts

questions.q: May you take this try?
choices: No; the month's tries are gone
No; the week's tries are gone
Yes; every trigger is a new trade
Yes, with a wider stop this time
questions.answer: No; the month's tries are gone
questions.why: No. A new trigger after a failed try is a new trade. But the cap is 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. You have already taken 6 this month.
questions.lesson_line: A new trigger is a new trade, but the cap still holds.

wrong.Yes; every trigger is a new trade: A new trigger is a new trade, but there is a cap: 6 tries a month on one stock.
wrong.No; the week's tries are gone: Two this week is under the cap of 3 tries a week. The month is what is used up.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: A wider stop does not lift the cap. The limit is 6 tries a month on one stock.

questions.story: This month you took six Remount tries on one stock, two of them this week. All hit the stop. Today it triggers again.
questions.simple: No, because we allow at most 6 tries a month on one stock and you have used all 6.

deeper.trap: Each new trigger is its own trade with its own stop, and that is the trap. The cap of 3 tries a week and 6 a month still counts every try on that stock. A wider stop is never the way back in.

reasons: +2 the try cap rests on the account rulebook
+1 fixed before

questions.q: After a stop-out, a second Remount try is a new trade with its own trigger and its own stop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop. A second try is a new trade with its own trigger and stop, at most 3 a week and 6 a month on one stock. It is not a rescue of the first trade.
questions.lesson_line: A second try is a new trade, not a rescue.
questions.simple: True. After a stop-out you may try again only on a new trigger, and the try is a fresh trade with its own stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21 and E56)
